live.name: NICKEL KIMBALL
live.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL: a threat actor tracked under many names
live.in_short: NICKEL KIMBALL is the Secureworks name for an actor also known as Kimsuky and APT43. The catalogue lists its aliases and tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL KIMBALL is the name Secureworks uses for this threat actor.
Other vendors track it under many other names, including APT43, Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, Velvet Chollima, THALLIUM, TA427 and Black Banshee.
The catalogue lists eight tools tied to the actor: BabyShark, FastFire, FastSpy, FireViewer, KONNI, KimJongRAT, Kimsuky and ReconShark.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: NICKEL KIMBALL
next.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL (Kimsuky): a North Korea-linked espionage group that favours phishing, trojanised installers and fake…
next.in_short: Vendors and officials link NICKEL KIMBALL, widely known as Kimsuky, to North Korea. Reports describe phishing, trojanised installers and Android spyware aimed mostly at South Korean targets. Attribution varies by source and confidence.

sentences.t: The catalogue lists many names for NICKEL KIMBALL, including Kimsuky, APT43, Emerald Sleet, Velvet Chollima, Springtail and THALLIUM.

Symantec describes Springtail, also called Kimsuky, as a North Korean espionage group. Symantec reports that the U.S. government has said the group is a unit of North Korea's military intelligence organization.
Breakglass Intelligence attributes a Kimsuky command server to the group with high confidence and calls it a DPRK actor.
According to a Sekoia and Kudelski Security overview, some DPRK experts regard Kimsuky as a mega-cluster made up of several branches, such as TA406 and TA408.

Genians says the KONNI campaign overlaps with Kimsuky and APT37 in targets and infrastructure, and some researchers class them as one group. Genians cites an MSMT report that assesses Kimsuky and KONNI as distinct groups.

Genians Security Center assesses with moderate confidence that Kimsuky ran a campaign against South Korean policy and security professionals. It notes that a third party imitating the same techniques cannot be ruled out.
Microsoft says Kimsuky has targeted people in international affairs organisations, NGOs, government agencies and media companies, in limited attacks since January 2025.
AhnLab reported signs of AppleSeed, a backdoor it says Kimsuky mainly uses, being spread to maintenance contractors of a military unit in July 2022.

South Korea's National Police Agency said Kimsuky exploited an email server flaw at a defense subcontractor between April and July 2023. The flaw allowed large files to be downloaded without logging in.
South Korea's National Cyber Security Center said Kimsuky compromised a construction trade organisation's website in January 2024 to spread trojanised security installers.

AhnLab says Kimsuky distributes shortcut (LNK) files disguised as ordinary documents, attached to spear-phishing emails with double extensions. The chain uses PowerShell and a Dropbox and TCP socket command channel to install the PebbleDash backdoor.

Microsoft says Kimsuky has adopted ClickFix-style tactics. A target who has been in contact with a fake South Korean official receives a PDF and is told to run code in PowerShell as administrator, which installs a remote desktop tool.

Symantec reports that Springtail has focused on trojanized software installers. It also describes Linux.Gomir, a Linux backdoor that appears to be a version of the Windows GoBear backdoor and supports 17 commands.

ENKI WhiteHat attributes new DOCSWAP Android malware to Kimsuky, citing shared infrastructure, a known phishing string and Korean comments. It says the apps posed as delivery services and carried a remote access tool with keylogging, and that it could not confirm how they were delivered.

Breakglass Intelligence describes a three-stage chain that starts from a CHM help file disguised as API documentation. It covers reconnaissance, a PowerShell bridge and a keylogger with clipboard monitoring.

In December 2022, South Korean officials said hackers believed to be operating from North Korea breached the internal network of the nuclear research body KAERI through a VPN server flaw. One of thirteen IP addresses abusing the flaw was linked to Kimsuky infrastructure.

In January 2021, ESRC research reported that Thallium altered the installer of a private stock investment messaging app to deliver malicious code. The researchers said the motive was unclear, whether money or espionage on traders.
ESRC linked a February 2022 Word lure posing as a Klip wallet customer-center guide to Thallium, also known as Kimsuky. The command server could not be reached, so analysis stopped there.
Treat unexpected shortcut files, help files and macro documents with suspicion, and never paste commands into PowerShell because a message asks you to.
